metadata.title: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
metadata.subject: Economics
metadata.objective: Show opportunity costs, specialization gains, and a range of beneficial terms of trade.
misconceptions: Absolute advantage determines gains from trade
One country must lose in every trade
expectedUnderstanding: Opportunity cost is what must be given up to produce one more unit.
A has a lower opportunity cost for cloth and B has a lower opportunity cost for wheat.
Specialization raises total output of both goods in this example.
Mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the two opportunity costs, and gains need not be equal.

primitives.text: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
Lower opportunity cost: A for cloth, B for wheat. Absolute output alone does not decide.
Total wheat: 15 at split, up to 20 with specialization
Total cloth: 15 at split, up to 20 with specialization
Terms of trade: 1 wheat for 0.5 to 2 cloth. Example 1 for 1 helps both; gains need not be equal.

checkpoints.title: Read opportunity cost
checkpoints.body: For A, one wheat costs two cloth, so one cloth costs half a wheat. For B, one wheat costs half a cloth, so one cloth costs two wheat.

checkpoints.title: Find comparative advantage
checkpoints.body: A gives up less cloth to make cloth, and B gives up less wheat to make wheat. Those lower opportunity costs decide specialization, not absolute output alone.

checkpoints.title: Specialize and trade
checkpoints.body: Both totals rise from 15 to 20. Any wheat price between 0.5 and 2 cloth can benefit both, such as 1 for 1. The gains need not be equal.

narration.text: Start with what each producer gives up. A can make 10 wheat or 20 cloth, so one wheat costs A two cloth. B can make 20 wheat or 10 cloth, so one wheat costs B half a cloth.
A has the lower opportunity cost for cloth. B has the lower opportunity cost for wheat. Absolute output alone does not decide who should specialize.
As production moves toward specialization, total wheat and total cloth both rise from 15 to 20. Trade at a price between the two opportunity costs can help both, but the gains need not be equal.

fallback.text: A can produce 10 wheat or 20 cloth, so one wheat costs A 2 cloth and one cloth costs A 0.5 wheat. B can produce 20 wheat or 10 cloth, so one wheat costs B 0.5 cloth and one cloth costs B 2 wheat. A has comparative advantage in cloth and B in wheat. Moving from split production to specialization raises both totals from 15 to 20. Terms of trade between 0.5 and 2 cloth per wheat can benefit both, with gains not necessarily equal.

accessibility.alt: Production table compares A, which can make 10 wheat or 20 cloth, with B, which can make 20 wheat or 10 cloth, including opportunity costs. A specializes in cloth and B in wheat. A slider raises total output bars from 15 to 20 for both goods.
